title: Directed, Weighted, and Other Flavours
excerpt: Direction, weight and shape each change which algorithms are available to you. Trees and DAGs get their own names because of how much follows from two short conditions.

content.text: The last page treated every edge as the same kind of thing. Real problems are fussier. Sometimes a connection runs one way only, sometimes it carries a cost, and sometimes the graph has a shape special enough to deserve its own name and its own faster algorithms.
This page is about those distinctions. Each one changes which algorithms are available to you, so it is worth being able to classify a graph before you start writing code against it.
In an undirected graph an edge between A and B means the two are connected, with no orientation attached, and friendship works like this: if you are my friend, then I am yours.
In a
directed

graph, often shortened to digraph, each edge points. An edge from A to B says nothing whatsoever about getting from B to A. Following someone on social media works this way, and so do one-way streets, web links, and "this task must finish before that one".

Direction is not a cosmetic detail. It breaks a property you have been quietly relying on. In an undirected graph, reachability is symmetric: if you can get to me, I can get to you, so "who is in my group" has a single clean answer. Take that away and the question splits in two,
who can I reach
and
who can reach me
, and the answers can be completely different sets.

That split is why directed graphs need their own machinery. Finding groups of mutually reachable nodes stops being one traversal and becomes Tarjan's algorithm, which is a later page in this section and would make no sense at all on undirected input.
A weighted graph attaches a number to each edge, usually a cost such as kilometers, milliseconds, money, or risk, though occasionally it is a capacity or a probability instead.

Adding weights changes what "shortest" means, and that single change is enough to retire an algorithm. Breadth-first search finds the route with the fewest edges, which stops being the cheapest route the moment the edges differ in cost. Three short hops can easily beat one long one. That is exactly the gap Dijkstra's algorithm exists to close.

Negative weights are a further step again, and they break Dijkstra rather than merely inconveniencing it. If a weight can be negative then adding more edges to a route can make it cheaper, and every argument that let Dijkstra commit to an answer early collapses. Bellman-Ford handles that case and pays for it in time.

body.text: Trees, and why they are worth naming

content.text: A
tree
is a graph that is connected and has no cycles. That is the whole definition, and it is worth pausing on how much follows from two short conditions.

The first consequence is that there is exactly one path between any two nodes. If there were two different paths you could go out along one and back along the other, which is a cycle, and trees do not have those. If there were none the graph would not be connected. Exactly one, always.
The second is that a tree on
n
nodes has precisely
edges. Start with one node and no edges. Every additional node needs exactly one edge to attach it to what is already there: fewer and it is disconnected, more and you have closed a loop.
That gives a genuinely useful test. Connected, acyclic, and
edges are three properties, and any two of them force the third.

body.code:
Connected?   Acyclic?   Edges = n-1?     Verdict
   yes          yes           yes          a tree
   yes          yes           no           impossible
   yes          no            yes          impossible
   no           yes           yes          impossible

Any two of the three force the third.

content.text: So checking whether something is a tree is easy: count the edges, then run one traversal to confirm it is connected. If both hold you are done, with no cycle detection required.

Trees turn up so often that people forget they are graphs at all. Your file system is one. The DOM is another. A binary search tree is obviously one. Anything you have written a recursive function over was probably a tree, and every graph algorithm in this section works on trees without modification, usually faster, because there are no cycles to guard against.
One warning about vocabulary. Trees in computer science usually have a designated
root

and talk about parents and children, but rooting is a choice you make rather than a property the graph has. Any node of a tree can be picked as the root, and the parent relationships rearrange themselves around your choice. A graph theorist's tree has no root at all.
Combine the two ideas: a directed graph with no directed cycles, which everyone calls a
DAG
DAGs are what you get whenever the edges mean must come before: build dependencies, course prerequisites, spreadsheet formulas, task schedules, and the order you put clothes on.

body.code:
shirt -> tie -> jacket          A valid order:
shirt -> belt                     socks, shirt, tie, trousers,
trousers -> belt                  belt, shoes, jacket
trousers -> shoes
socks -> shoes                  Another valid order:
                                  shirt, tie, socks, trousers,
No cycles, so an order exists.    shoes, belt, jacket

content.text: The absence of cycles is precisely what makes those problems solvable. A cycle would mean A must precede B, which must precede C, which must precede A, and no ordering can satisfy that. When a build system tells you it found a circular dependency, it is telling you your graph is not a DAG, so your question has no answer. Finding a valid order is topological sorting, which is the next page.
Switch between the tabs. Same nodes each time, different rules about what the edges mean, and completely different questions worth asking.
A
self-loop
is an edge from a node to itself. A
multigraph
allows several edges between the same pair of nodes, which matters when the edges are genuinely distinct, as the seven bridges of Konigsberg were.

Most algorithms and most problem statements quietly assume neither exists. That assumption is usually safe, and when it is wrong it tends to produce a confusing bug rather than a crash, so it is worth checking the constraints of a problem before assuming a clean simple graph.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 12 nodes and 11 edges. What must it be?

options.label: A tree, because connected plus n-1 edges forces acyclic
A DAG, though possibly not a tree

questions.prompt: Why does making a graph directed require new algorithms for finding groups?

options.label: Reachability stops being symmetric, so who I can reach and who can reach me are different questions
Directed graphs can have more edges

options.label: The dependency graph contains a directed cycle, so it is not a DAG and no valid build order exists
Two files were given the same node

seoTitle: Types of Graphs: Directed, Weighted, DAG, and Tree
seoDescription: Directed and undirected graphs, weighted edges, trees and DAGs explained: why direction splits reachability in two, why a tree on n nodes has n-1 edges, and why cycles make ordering impossible.
